newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek election turns suddenly into two-horse race.
newsitem.headline: Greek election turns suddenly into two-horse race.

text.p: Greece's opposition conservatives, showering voters with populist promises, are in a neck-and-neck race with the country's ruling socialists less than two weeks before national elections, opinion polls showed on Monday.
What had been a sleepy campaign, with more than 50 percent of voters saying they had little or no interest in the outcome, has suddenly turned dramatic.
The first campaign polls show the conservatives, led by Miltiades Evert, in striking distance of an upset victory, largely because of the surprising strength of several smaller leftwing parties.
"The opinion polls show the September 22 election will not be an easy walkover for the ruling socialists," Eleftherotypia newspaper said.

"When the (snap) election was called (Prime Minister) Costas Simitis seemed to catch the opposition by surprise. It now seems the socialists were caught by surprise too because they couldn't quickly mobilise and start their campaign," it said.

A weekend MRB poll gave the conservatives 31 percent of the vote and the socialists 30.6 percent. A separate poll by the PRC firm had the socialists with 32.8 percent and the conservatives with 31.9 percent.
Most striking was the strength of smaller leftwing parties, which are digging into the vote of the socialist rank and file, setting off alarm bells in the socialist camp.
A new leftist party set up by ex-socialist finance minister Dimitris Tsovolas had between 5.2 and six percent of the vote in the poll -- all coming from the governing party's supporters.
The Left Coalition party of Nikos Konstandopoulos, which failed to win a seat in the November 1993 election, had between 4.2 and 5.3 percent -- again, much coming from the traditional socialist vote.
Tsovolas, a grassroots socialist known for his "give it all away" approach to economics, and Konstandopoulos, a respected lawyer, rated as the two most popular politicians in the polls.
That popularity and their devotion to a welfare state may keep their followers faithful and prevent them from moving into the ruling socialist fold on election day.

In contrast Simitis, 60, appears almost conservative in his commitment to strict measures to ensure EU economic targets are met. He has failed to excite voters with a deadpan professorial style and his precise lectures on the importance of EU goals.
The socialists have been criticised for running a complacent campaign, smug and self-assured of victory until the polls.
"We've just begun our contact with the voters," said former socialist transport minister Thanasis Tsouras. "It's too bad we didn't do it from the start. Television isn't enough."
Evert, 57, son of an Athens police chief, has run a populist campaign offering generous perks to one and all, and denouncing Simitis as a neo-conservative on economic policy.
He has offered a better deal for farmers and a bonus for state pensioners and told the residents of Athens Korydallos area he would close down a local maximum security prison.
Known as the "Bulldozer" for his "Just Do It" style, Evert has plunged into the campaign with a passion, clearly enjoying pressing the flesh or chanting along with campaign crowds.
"Our main asset is that Mr Evert touches the simple folks, Mr Simitis is not capable of doing this," conservative New Democracy deputy Michalis Liapis said.
If that proves true, then calling the snap election will be the biggest mistake of Simitis' short tenure as prime minister.
He cited trouble with Turkey and a fragile economy as his reason for calling an election a year early but he also intended to cement his grip on power within his party and the country.
An economist and lawyer by training, Simitis was elected premier by his parliamentary group in January after the late socialist party founder Andreas Papandreou resigned in poor health.
Simitis proved himself a masterful tactician in winning the premiership and then the socialist leadership but he has yet to lead his party to a national election win.
